data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference is a 'critical convention': we choose the better-corroborated theory specifically because it is more falsifiable, thus exposing ourselves to greater risk of error, which is the opposite of inductive safety.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If scientists actually prefer safe, low-content theories in practice.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'learning velocity' cannot justify the high costs of acting on potentially false theories.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'boldness' of a theory is independent of its corroboration status.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Induction seeks safety and high probability. Popperian preference seeks high content and high falsifiability. A well-corroborated theory is often the bold one that stuck its neck out and survived. We prefer it not because it is 'safe' (inductive) but because it offers the most leverage for future refutation. If it fails, we learn more. The preference is defensible as a strategy for maximizing learning velocity, not for minimizing error probability. The cost of accepting this is admitting that science aims for rapid failure and replacement, not cumulative certainty.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
